newsitem.title: USA: S&P-sovereign ceiling ratings policy not abolished.
newsitem.headline: S&P-sovereign ceiling ratings policy not abolished.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said in a teleconference that it had not ended its sovereign ceiling ratings policy despite granting some corporate issuers in Argentina higher ratings than those of their home country.

"In the case of many dollarized economies, we haven't abolished the sovereign ceiling ... we have relaxed it to the extent of two notches," said David Beers, managing director and head of the sovereign ratings group at Standard & Poor's.

Last week, S&P said it concluded sovereign credit risk in certain dollarized countries is less a factor in assessing the creditworthiness of corporate issuers. Dollarization refers to the process of replacing the local currency with U.S. dollars as the main vehicle for savings and investment.
The rating agency subsequently upgraded several Argentine issuers by as much as two levels above the republic's double-B rating.
Asked why S&P decided on a two-notch limit to the ratings adjustments, Beers said it was "really a judgment call."
"It was a pragmatic decision that we made, but one we will be keeping under close review to the extent that we see going forward that our fundamental premise is proving to be accurate," he said.

The teleconference represented an attempt to correct misperceptions about the ratings changes, Beers said. In particular, many people have mistakenly associated dollarization with dollar convertability.
"Our policy does not rely on the fact of the exchange-rate policy of Argentina," Beers said.
"The vast majority of dollarized countries -- like Russia, Turkey, Lebanon, Peru, Bolivia and Uruguay -- do not have fixed exchange rates with the U.S. dollar," he added.
Even if the Argentine peso were to depreciate against the dollar, private-sector issuers in the republic would most likely retain access to foreign exchange for debt servicing, Beers said.
S&P said its policy revision will also affect some issuers in Panama and Uruguay, and probably other dollarized nations as well.
In addition, the rating agency said it would consider higher-than-sovereign ratings for firms in non-dollarized economies if they have a high ratio of overseas earnings.
"We would look for the balance of risk where the cash flows are generated," said Lacey Gallagher, director of sovereign ratings.
"We don't see exempting exporters in general," she added. "We've seen too many cases in non-dollarized economies where a sovereign default does, in fact, enforce exchange control."
